titulo.texto: Polychrome Vessel of the Zaachila Hummingbird

frase_gancho.texto: A tiny bird peers over the rim of a cup taken from a royal tomb.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the finest clay we move on to the brightest metal. Look for the gold jewelry of the Mixtec tradition: small ornaments made for the chest, the ears, or the lip, some with bells or pendants.

guion_corto.texto: This little clay bird peers over the rim of a cup as if it were about to drink. It is a hummingbird, and the cup, made of fine clay polished until it shines, measures about eight centimeters. It is decorated with red, white, black, gray, and blue pigments. It came from the tombs of Zaachila, in Oaxaca, a city where Zapotecs and Mixtecs lived side by side. It dates to the Postclassic, the last centuries before the arrival of the Spanish. For specialists, the hummingbird was a bird of the Sun and could represent a ruler. It has also been proposed that it is the Sun itself, drinking the blood of sacrifices. The cup may have been an offering, although it is not ruled out that someone drank from it.

guion_largo.texto:
In January of 1962, the archaeologist Roberto Gallegos Ruiz had been excavating for about two and a half weeks at El Cerrito, an area of Zaachila, in Oaxaca. Suddenly they noticed a crack in a stucco floor. Beneath it was a tomb. When Gallegos entered the main chamber, he saw a skeleton, a gold ring, and, beside them, this cup. He himself has said that at that moment he did not know the importance of what lay before him.

Zaachila was a city of Zapotecs and Mixtecs. According to the INAH, from the middle of the twelfth century there were alliances among their royal houses. The tombs opened in 1962 date to the Postclassic, and from them came a little over one hundred twenty-five pieces that reached this museum. In Tomb 1, nine people were counted, although their bones had almost crumbled away. That number has been linked to the nine levels of the underworld.

Look at the cup slowly. It measures about eight centimeters and fits in the palm of a hand. It is made of fine, burnished clay, that is, rubbed until the surface shines. On the rim, the artist modeled a hummingbird. One catalog speaks of the delicacy and grace of this piece, and it is hard not to agree.

Why a hummingbird? Today we see it as a tender bird. For the ancient peoples of Mexico it was something else: a bird of the Sun. The curator Martha Carmona has explained that here it may represent a ruler with solar traits. She has also said that the turquoise blue of the original cup was read as a sign of divine power. Another reading proposes that the bird that drinks is the Sun itself, drinking the blood of sacrifices.

That idea may sound familiar if you passed through the Mexica Hall. There you met Huitzilopochtli, the god of the Sun and of war, whose name is interpreted as «left-handed hummingbird». It was believed that fallen warriors accompanied the Sun and that, after four years, they returned transformed into hummingbirds and butterflies. The Zaachila cup belongs to another people and another era, but it shares that intuition. A tiny bird could carry the entire weight of the Sun.

What was it for? We do not fully know. It has been thought to be a vessel for offerings, although it is not ruled out that it was used for drinking in some ceremony. What we do know is that it was in the main chamber of a tomb, next to a gold ring. That says a great deal about who owned it. There is another tomb in Zaachila, Tomb 2. There, the principal lord wore a great gold pectoral, a bead necklace, and obsidian ear ornaments, and other figures had bracelets and rings. It is the world of jewelry that you will see at the next stop.

The cup also had a second life. The Mexican Baseball League gives its champion a trophy inspired by it, with a hummingbird on the rim. It is called the Zaachila Cup. A piece from a Mixtec tomb now lends its name to a baseball trophy.

Before moving on, look once more at the hummingbird’s beak. The whole meaning of the piece fits in that gesture: a tiny bird, about to drink.

texto: Find the hummingbird modeled on the rim of the cup
Notice the painted colors and the shine of the polished clay
Look at the hummingbird’s beak: does it lean toward the inside of the cup?

texto.Material: Codex-style polychrome ceramic (fine burnished clay with red, white, black, gray, and Maya blue pigments)
texto.Origin: Tomb 1 of Zaachila, Oaxaca (explored by Roberto Gallegos in 1962)
texto.Dimensions: 7.5 cm high x 7.8 cm in diameter

texto.pregunta: Myth: For the ancient peoples of Mexico, the hummingbird was a symbol of tenderness.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was a bird of the Sun, linked to rulers and warriors; the Mexica god of war had a name that is interpreted as «left-handed hummingbird».
